issues.title: Handshake Context for supplemental authentication is not defined
issues.author: tireddy2
issues.body:
The draft describes transcript construction for supplemental authentication, but it does not explicitly define this in terms of the Handshake Context defined in Section 4.4 of TLS 1.3. 

The draft should explicitly define the Handshake Context used for supplemental authentication sequences.

a) The Handshake Context will differ between the client and the server, consistent with the Table in Section 4.4.
b) The Handshake Context should include the CertificateRequest message that carries the supplemental_certificate_requests extension.

Previously transmitted supplemental authentication messages would become part of the evolving Handshake Context, so that each subsequent CertificateVerify and Finished computation includes them.

Apart from the definition of the Handshake Context, the construction of CertificateVerify and Finished should follow the same rules defined in Section 4.4 of TLS 1.3.

issues.title: Compatibility with QUIC post-handshake restrictions
issues.author: tireddy2
issues.body:
RFC 9001 states that servers MUST NOT use post-handshake client authentication and specifically:

servers MUST NOT send post-handshake TLS CertificateRequest messages, and clients MUST treat receipt of such messages as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

Since this draft introduces additional Certificate, CertificateVerify, and Finished authentication sequences after the handshake, it is unclear how this mechanism would operate over QUIC without violating the QUIC-TLS restriction.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body: QUIC-TLS prohibits Post Handshake Authentication as specified in RFC8446 because authentication context potentially changes after QUIC handshake and this change might apply to different streams differently. This proposal does not have this problem.

issues.title: Impact of supplemental authentication on the TLS key schedule
issues.author: tireddy2
issues.body: It does not describe the impact of these post-handshake supplemental authentication messages on the TLS key schedule.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body: Post handshake supplemental authentication messages do not affect TLS key schedule. Do you think it needs to be spelled out?

comments.author: tireddy2
comments.body:
> Post handshake supplemental authentication messages do not affect TLS key schedule. Do you think it needs to be spelled out?

I think it needs to be discussed. 

Unlike composite certificates presented during the main handshake where the certificate is used in the handshake transcript and is used to derive secrets; supplemental certificates arrive after the key schedule is finalized and therefore do not contribute to any derived keys. We will have to analyze threats possible because of this distinction, for instance, when a traditional certificate is compromised but the PQC certificate is not: an attacker acting as MiTM can complete a valid handshake using the compromised traditional certificate and omits the supplemental PQC authentication flight entirely, effectively a downgrade attack.

To mitigate this, endpoints will have to enforce a local policy that prohibits accepting a connection authenticated solely with a traditional certificate when a PQC supplemental certificate is required,

issues.title: max_certificates
issues.author: rifaat-ietf
issues.body:
I was wondering about your choice of using max_certificates.

How would a server, for example, explicitly require the client to provide exactly two certificates:
A traditional certificate and PQC certificate? or 
A user certificate and a device certificate?

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body:
`max_certificates` applies to each `SupplementalCertificateRequest`. In your example, the server will request one client certificate via the `CertificateRequest` itself and exactly one supplemental certificate by including `supplemental_certificate_requests` with `max_certificates`=1 in the only `CertificateRequest`.

But if there are up to 3 device attestation certificates that server would like to accept from the client (in addition to user cert) it would send `CertificateRequest ` for the user cert with `supplemental_certificate_requests` extension containing one `SupplementalCertificateRequest` with `max_certificates`=3

comments.author: rifaat-ietf
comments.body:
max_certificates implies that the party that sent the request is willing to accept no certificates at all. For example, if max_certificates=1 it implies that the party is willing to accept a maximum of 1 certificate, which includes no certificate.

If this is not the intention, then maybe we need to find a better name for this parameter.
If it is intentional, then this implies that the application is required to enforce whatever policy it wants at a later stage.

Both valid, and have pros and cons.

issues.title: Policy Section
issues.author: rifaat-ietf
issues.body:
# Application Policy Enforcement

Applications making use of supplemental authentication must define a clear and unambiguous policy for interpreting the set of authentication statements presented in the TLS handshake and subsequent supplemental authentication flights. This policy dictates the requirements for establishing a connection and for granting access to specific resources.
When evaluating a connection, the application's policy engine must consider all received authentication statements, as well as the absence of expected statements, as inputs to its authorization decision. Incorrect or incomplete policy evaluation can lead to severe security vulnerabilities.

Endpoints should perform their complete policy evaluation after all supplemental authentication flights are complete and before processing any application data. If the full set of presented identities does not satisfy the application's policy, the endpoint must terminate the connection, preferably with a specific alert (e.g., bad_certificate or access_denied).


# Policy Enforcement Scenarios

The following non-normative examples illustrate how application policy interacts with the supplemental authentication mechanism.

## Hybrid Post-Quantum and Traditional Authentication

A high-security client has a local policy requiring that all connections to a specific server be mutually authenticated using both a traditional ECDSA certificate and a post-quantum ML-DSA certificate.

- Client Policy: Connection requires client authentication with both an ECDSA certificate and a ML-DSA certificate.

- Handshake: The server sends a CertificateRequest message.

    Success: The server includes the supplemental_certificate_requests extension. The main request asks for an ECDSA certificate, and a supplemental request asks for a ML-DSA certificate. The client is able to satisfy both and proceeds.

    Failure: The server's CertificateRequest only asks for an ECDSA certificate and does not include a supplemental request for ML-DSA. Upon receiving the CertificateRequest, the client's policy engine determines that its mandatory requirement for dual authentication cannot be met. The client must abort the handshake by sending a handshake_failure alert. It is a policy violation to proceed with a connection that is only partially authenticated according to its own requirements.

## Device and User Identity

A service provider uses supplemental authentication to separate device and user identity for a remote access service. The policy grants different levels of access based on the combination of identities presented.

Server Policy:

- Any connection requires a valid, corporate-managed device certificate.
- Access to the general user portal requires a valid user certificate in addition to the device certificate.
- Access to the admin portal requires a valid user certificate with the "admin" role, in addition to the device certificate.


Handshake: 

The server sends a CertificateRequest asking for the device certificate in the main handshake and includes a supplemental_certificate_requests extension asking for a user certificate.

Server Action:

- If a client provides only a valid device certificate, the connection is established, but the application will deny access to any resource pending the user authentication. 
- If a client provides a valid device certificate and a valid standard user certificate, the application grants access to the general user portal but denies access to the admin portal.
- If a client provides a valid device certificate and a valid admin user certificate, the application grants access to both portals.
- If a client provides an invalid device certificate, the server must abort the handshake, regardless of what user certificate is offered. The primary authentication failed to meet the baseline policy.

issues.title: One-sided Handshake Context
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body:
From @yaronf review:

> Section 6.2 excludes peer supplemental authentication messages from each
endpoint's Handshake Context so that both sides can send concurrently.
Is there precedent for this in TLS 1.3? The asymmetry feels risky and
deserves explicit justification.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body:
@yaronf yes, such precedent exists in TLS 1.3 key schedule. application traffic secrets and main secret only use ClientHello..*server* Finished, while resumption main secret uses ClientHello..*client* Finished.
Without this asymmetry this mechanism will incur at least one additional RTT. This may be a necessary sacrifice for the security, but I'd rather do that only under FATT guidance (if we get to that)

issues.author: yaroslavros

> "When accepted, one or more supplemental authentication flights may be
sent after the handshake and before the sender transmits application
data" — who is the sender here? In bidirectional supplemental
authentication, both endpoints may send flights. This also raises
implementation questions the draft does not address, such as when an
application is notified (e.g., via a callback) that the handshake has
completed.

issues.title: DTLS-specific concerns
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body:
From @yaronf review:

> Several aspects of the draft may not carry over cleanly to DTLS:
> 
> - Section 3 states that an endpoint MUST NOT interleave application data
> or other TLS messages with supplemental authentication flights. DTLS ACK
> records should probably be carved out as an exception.
> - Requiring contiguous supplemental authentication flights and enforcing
> ordering via `unexpected_message` may be insufficient when datagrams
> arrive out of order. Section 7.2 may need additional mechanisms to
> ensure reordering does not break the protocol.
> - Section 7.6 requires that `NewSessionTicket` not be sent until all
> supplemental authentication sequences from both endpoints have

issues.title: Extension vs flag integrity guarantees conflated
issues.author: yaroslavros
issues.body:
From @yaronf review:

> Section 7.2 attributes sequence integrity to the
`supplemental_certificate` flag, but the extension also appears to
participate in the same guarantees (that sequences cannot be truncated
or reordered). Please clarify what each mechanism contributes.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body:
@yaronf not sure if I follow. What extension are you referring to?
Please take a look at https://github.com/yaroslavros/tls-supplemental-auth/pull/15 which tightens up extension/flag terminology. Does that resolve your concern?

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body: Now I'm confused: even with #15, the IANA section defines both an extension and a flag.

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body:
There is `supplemental_certificate_requests` extension defined in Section 4. It can be included in `ClientHello` and/or `CertificateRequest`. It indicates support for receiving supplemental certificates and, optionally, includes list of extensions/contexts similarly to CertificateRequest message.

There is `supplemental_certificate` TLS flag defined in Section 5. It can be included in `Certificate`. It indicates that there will be at least one more supplemental authentication flight.

I was hoping that introduction, examples and the rest of the draft text are clear enough... if not, anything you could suggest to improve the clarity?

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
This comment was specifically about this text:

> The supplemental_certificate TLS flag ensures that supplemental authentication sequences cannot be truncated or reordered without detection. If a Certificate message indicates that another supplemental authentication sequence will follow, the receiver expects the next message from that endpoint to begin the next sequence. Any deviation from this ordering results in a TLS protocol error.

I would have written it differently (I don't like the notion that the flag "ensures" state machine behavior). But it's not very important.

comments.author: yaroslavros

issues.title: Reject unreasonably high max_certificates
issues.author: yaroslavros

comments.author: yaroslavros
comments.body: @yaronf I'm not sure if I understand why would one want to reject high advertised value of `max_certificates`. This parameter is used to advertise how many supplemental certificate chains does the endpoint is ready to accept. If a client speaks to a server and server says - `max_certificates = 100` which means "feel free to send me up to 100 certificate chains" - it is not a threat to the client in any way. It is still free to send just one (or none).

comments.author: yaronf
